## Key Features {.unnumbered}

- **What is unique:** a large, fully simulated, multi-file dataset for linking individual people, with cross-file ground truth (every record carries a `simulant_id`, so missed-match and false-match rates of any method can be computed exactly), designed to capture the record-linkage challenges faced by a Florida-scale cancer data system.

- **Why created:** linkage software for cancer registries must be developed and tested on names, dates of birth, addresses and SSNs, which are exactly the identifiers that confidentiality rules prevent registries from releasing.

- **Details:** a simulated Florida drawn from the `{python} fl_pool` simulated people recorded as residents in the simulated 2020, 2030, or 2040 censuses, including a simulated registry of `{python} registry_rows` records whose age and sex distribution is that of the cases reported by the Florida Cancer Data System, and researcher "finder files" of `{python} finder_500k_rows` and `{python} finder_100k_rows` records drawn from residents in `{python} finder_year`.

- **Data linkage:** the larger finder file includes `{python} overlap_500k_target` people who are also in the registry and the smaller finder file includes `{python} overlap_100k_target`. There is no overlap between the finder files.

- **Main categories of data:** simulated person-level identifiers including name, date of birth, sex, street-address fields, SSN, race/ethnicity, and a diagnosis date on each registry record, carrying realistic synthetic noise (typos, nicknames, month/day swaps, blanks, duplications).

- **Access:** direct download under a permissive license with a DOI.

# Background {#sec-background}

Population-based cancer registries may be the single most valuable resource in cancer epidemiology [@parkin2006evolution]. A registry holds a record of every cancer diagnosed among the residents of a state or country, and the incidence and survival statistics that cancer control depends on come from those records, as does the evidence of disparities in detection and treatment. This is also the raw material for global estimates of cancer burden, which are assembled from every registry available [@gbd2023cancer]. A registry linked to other data also turns a cohort of exposed people (or a set of insurance claims) into a study with cancer as the outcome [@enewold2020seermedicare]. The Florida Cancer Data System (FCDS) is one such registry; it has collected cases statewide since 1981 and holds more than seven million records [@fcds_welcome].

Record linkage is how most of that value is derived from a registry [@howe1998linkage]. A researcher or a public health program has a list of people, such as a cohort of workers, the participants in a screening program, or the enrollees in a clinical trial, and needs to know which of them have cancer; the registry links the list to its records and reports the matches. This link can be made based on name, date of birth, address, or even Social Security number (SSN), all of which might be misspelled, out of date, or just missing in some of the records. But missing a match might make it appear that a person stayed healthy when really they developed cancer, while making a false match might make it appear that a person developed a cancer that never really occurred. Either error can produce misleading results [@harron2017challenges; @doidge2018demystifying]. 

Improving record linkage for cancer registries is hard because the data that they link is confidential and cannot be openly shared [@fdoh_fcds_procedure_guide_2007]. The confidentiality rules vary from state to state, but none allow sufficient sharing to openly optimize a linkage system [@naaccr2023secondarysharing]. Researchers have obtained access to confidential fields through lengthy approval processes, but this can take years and substantial expense [@buchanich2009methodological]. Furthermore, even if registry data is obtained, it does not come with any source of "ground truth" to show which records truly belong together, so the accuracy of a linkage can only be estimated, not measured [@harron2017guide]. Simulated data can avoid these issues, but so far have fallen short in other ways. The classic test corpora hold thousands of records, and the generators behind them struggle to go past a million records [@christen2008febrl; @tran2013geco; @hildebrandt2020dapo]. There are large, openly downloadable person files from voter rolls, but these contain only a handful of fields and no children [@saeedi2018famer; @binette2022almost]. The one cancer registry benchmark we know of contains comparison scores rather than records, so it cannot exercise blocking or string comparison [@schmidtmann2011krebsregister], and the one large microsimulation built to study linkage quality, about 20 million people in a German educational register, was not released with its papers as far as we can find [@schnell2023microsim]. The simulation this work builds on, pseudopeople, is not tuned to cancer demographics, and its large populations are available only on request [@keyes2026governance]. When FCDS evaluated open-source linkage software in 2023, they used a test file based on pseudopeople that was supplied privately, and in their report, they called for such data to be made more openly available [@alexandersson2023splinkfcds].

This data resource is our answer to the need for a large-scale dataset for improving cancer registry record linkage. It is a direct download under a DOI, with no request, approval, or data-use agreement required. Every record carries an identifier that says which person it describes, so the accuracy of a linkage can be measured rather than estimated. The files have the fields that real linkages run on, including SSNs and street addresses, at the scale of a state registry and with errors of the kinds and rates seen at FCDS. The demographics of the simulated data match the age and sex pattern of FCDS's reported cases, and the cohorts overlap the registry by precisely known amounts. Because every person in every file is simulated, there is nothing in this data resource that is confidential. The rest of this paper describes how the files were built (@sec-methods), what is in them and how hard they are to link (@sec-results), what they can and cannot stand in for (@sec-discussion), and how to get them (@sec-access).

# Methods {#sec-methods}

This section describes how we extracted a simulated Florida population (@sec-source), how we generated three files from that extract (@sec-design), how we noised each file and formatted them for release (@sec-noise), how we validated our work (@sec-qa), and a series of simple experiments on deterministic linkage that we ran on the simulated data (@sec-characterize).

## Source population and the Florida extract {#sec-source}

The records come from pseudopeople, a Python package for generating simulated versions of the data sets on which census-scale record linkage often runs [@pseudopeople_software; @haddock2024simulated]. It uses output from a dynamic microsimulation of the United States, initialized to the size and demographics of the country in 2020 and run forward through 2040 with births, deaths, and migration. Each simulated person (a "simulant" in pseudopeople's vocabulary) carries a `simulant_id` and is observed by simulated data-collecting systems, such as a decennial census in 2020, 2030, and 2040; Social Security's administrative data system; and tax filings [@haddock2024simulated]. The package ships with a small sample population, and populations the size of Rhode Island and of the USA are available on request [@keyes2026governance].

```{python}
#| label: psp-defaults
import pseudopeople as psp
psp_defaults = psp.get_config()["decennial_census"]
psp_cell_default = pct(psp_defaults["column_noise"]["first_name"]["make_typos"]["cell_probability"], 0)
psp_nonresponse = pct(psp_defaults["row_noise"]["do_not_respond"]["row_probability"], 2)
```

The package can generate one state's census data directly, but it does not offer the sampling design we needed, with quotas by age and sex and controlled overlaps between files, so we did the selection ourselves. We used DuckDB `{python} duckdb_version` to read the census observer's Parquet files directly, kept the Florida rows of the three censuses, one per person per census, and built two pools from them. We created a "last-seen pool" that holds every person ever recorded in Florida, taken once at their latest census, and is the frame for the simulated registry; it is more than twice the size of Florida's population at any one census, because it keeps everyone who died or left the state between censuses, which matches what a cancer registry contains. We used only the residents from `{python} finder_year` as the frame for the finder files, since a researcher's cohort is often a roster of living people at one time. We joined SSNs from the Social Security observer on the simulant identifier, and we then ran pseudopeople on only the rows we selected, which made the Florida-scale computation fast enough for iterative development. Addresses in the source are real Florida city names and ZIP codes with simulated streets, so the released addresses place people in real cities at no real location [@haddock2024simulated].

## Cohort design and sampling {#sec-design}

From these source populations, we sampled a simulated registry of `{python} cfg_registry_target` people with the age and sex distribution of the cases FCDS reported between 1995 and 2023 [@pseudopeople_issue205], and finder files of `{python} cfg_finder_500k_target` and `{python} cfg_finder_100k_target` people. We designed the sampling procedure so that `{python} overlap_500k_target` and `{python} overlap_100k_target` people in each finder file also appear in the registry, with no person in both finder files. The age and sex target is the count column of an FCDS table of reported cases by sex and `{python} n_age_groups` age groups, taken as shares [@fcds_general_incidence_2026]<!-- the second author extracted the table from FCDS; confirm the report parameters at source before publication (OUTLINE decision #7) -->, and each of the `{python} n_strata` strata contributes an exact quota, which we filled using a reproducible random draw within each stratum.

Since we sampled our finder files from the simulated `{python} finder_year` census, overlapping entries in the registry are only possible for registry members sampled from the `{python} finder_year` census as well. We switched off pseudopeople's row noise (non-response, row omission, and duplication), which drops or duplicates whole rows, so each file holds exactly the people we drew, and we drew the second finder file from the people the first had not taken, so the two share no one. This produced the ground truth for scoring: a registry row and a finder row that carry the same identifier form a true match, which a linkage should find, and every other pairing of a registry row with a finder row is a true non-match; people last seen in 2020 or 2030 appear in the registry alone, and are all non-matches a linkage should reject. Each true match represents one simulant recorded twice, with different noise for the registry and the finder files, and its two records differ only by injected noise, with no move, aging, or change of surname between them.

## Noise, schema, and packaging {#sec-noise}

We adapted pseudopeople's default noise suite, in which each column is corrupted sequentially by several mechanisms, each affecting `{python} psp_cell_default` of cells apiece (e.g. a first name can be left blank, replaced by a nickname or a fake name, and/or altered by a phonetic, optical-character-recognition, or typing error; a date of birth can have its month and day swapped, digits miswritten, and/or be copied from a household member; a categorical field can take a wrong category). As mentioned above, we switched off its row noise (@sec-design). We made two additional changes: first, we raised the blanking of the six address fields to `{python} cfg_finder_address_missing` in the finder files and left it at `{python} cfg_registry_address_missing` in the registry. Second, we noised the SSN ourselves, by (1) blanking SSNs to a target share of `{python} cfg_finder_ssn_missing` in the finder files and `{python} cfg_registry_ssn_missing` in the registry, counting the people who never held a number in the simulation before blanking anyone else; and (2) swapping one adjacent pair of digits in `{python} cfg_finder_ssn_transposed` of the finder files' remaining SSNs, a noise mechanism that pseudopeople currently does not offer. We selected these rates based on experience with what typical finder files look like compared to the registry file, which is usually the cleaner of the two [@qiao2023lexisnexis]. Several kinds of real-world error are absent: we gave the SSN no wrong digits and did not replace any SSN with a relative's number, we include no name changes to surnames, we applied the noise independently across files and fields, and we wrote all files in one consistent format.

Every row of each file contains its `simulant_id` identifier as well as the fields that linkage typically relies on: first name, middle initial, last name, date of birth, sex, race/ethnicity, street number, street name, unit number, city, state, ZIP code, and SSN (we included race/ethnicity because FCDS's submission layout carries it [@fcds_linkage_layout]). This captures every field in both of FCDS's minimum matching sets, but does not include some of their optional fields, such as maiden name, alias, or birthplace. We gave each registry row a diagnosis date, a day drawn uniformly within the year of the record's census, so that age at diagnosis is within a year of the age the quota was matched on, at the cost that diagnoses heap on three years. Since the finder files are cohort rosters, we gave them no such date. We wrote the files in comma-separated value (CSV) format, with a header row and empty fields for blanks, and packaged the three CSV files with a data dictionary (every field's format, blank convention, and noise mechanisms) in a zip built so that its bytes depend only on its contents; the deposit carries beside it a manifest of MD5 and SHA-256 hashes for each file and the configuration file with every seed and noise target. This profile describes dataset version `{python} dataset_version`, which we built with pseudopeople `{python} psp_version`.

## Quality assurance {#sec-qa}

We developed four checks to run on this data for verification and validation purposes. To check reproducibility, since the build is intended to be a deterministic result of the configuration's seeds, we built the release twice and compared the hash digests of every file. To check the data scale, we compared the 2020 extract with Florida's official 2020 census count [@census2020_table2]. To check the composition of the population, we computed the age and sex composition of each file from the source's true ages (rather than the noised dates of birth) and compared the registry's demographic pattern with the FCDS shares we intended it to match, recording the largest deviation of any stratum, and compared the finder files' composition with that of the `{python} finder_year` Florida pool. To further check the face validity of the data, we tabulated the three most common first names in each age and sex group and examined a sample of true matches side by side.

## Characterizing the data {#sec-characterize}

Finally, we ran several simple computations on the released files. First, we examined the error structure of the files: for each field, we measured the share of blank values in each file against the rate we set for it and, among true matches, the share whose two values are present and identical character for character, as well as the share with a blank on either side. We also counted the finder-file SSNs with two adjacent digits swapped and we ran sentinel checks for several specific noise types: dates of birth that do not parse as calendar dates, Doe-pattern names, repeated-digit SSNs, and SSNs outside the ranges the Social Security Administration issues. We also tabulated SSN blankness by race/ethnicity and by age at diagnosis.

Second, we measured the uniqueness of combinations of attributes, such as the share of registry people who have a unique combination of first name, last name, and date of birth; of last name and date of birth; or of ZIP code, date of birth, and sex. We also measured the fraction of the population who share a full name with someone else.

Third, as a baseline, we conducted deterministic record linkage for `{python} n_rules` exact-agreement rules, each requiring agreement on either one set of fields or on at least one of two sets of fields, after lower-casing and trimming. We measured precision and recall, which we also report as false-match and missed-match rates [@lam2024synthetic]; we did not rank rules by F1 [@hand2018fmeasure] and we omit specificity, which is uninformative when true non-matches grow with the product of the file sizes [@christen2007quality]. We included the two field sets that the FCDS Procedure Guide requires in a submission [@fdoh_fcds_procedure_guide_2007] as well as the two in the Data Linkage Record Layout [@fcds_linkage_layout]. We also examined stratified precision and recall scores for three of the deterministic linkage rules within the race/ethnicity groups of the finder record [@mcgrathlone2021ethnicbias].

Finally, we investigated the computational demand of two blocking rules [@christen2007quality], by counting the number of candidate pairs and the share of true matches retained when comparisons are restricted to records that agree on the full date of birth, or on the first letter of the last name with the year of birth.

# Results {#sec-results}

We describe the released files first (@sec-structure), then the simulants in them (@sec-population), the errors in their fields (@sec-errors) and how hard those errors make the files to link with exact rules (@sec-difficulty).

## Structure, contents, and where the data are held {#sec-structure}

This data resource is a zip archive containing three comma-separated data files and a data dictionary, to be deposited on Zenodo under a DOI that will be minted before publication<!-- OUTLINE run-list item 10 -->. The high-level characteristics of the files are described in @tbl-release: a simulated registry of `{python} registry_simulants` people and two finder files of `{python} finder_500k_simulants` and `{python} finder_100k_simulants` people. All three are drawn from Florida residents in the simulated 2020, 2030, or 2040 census, a pool of `{python} fl_pool` distinct simulated people. The larger finder file shares `{python} overlap_500k_simulants` people with the registry, `{python} pct(match_prevalence_500k, 0)` of its records, and the smaller shares `{python} overlap_100k_simulants`, the same `{python} pct(match_prevalence_100k, 0)` share; the two finder files share no people with each other, matching the overlap design described above (@sec-design).

The data dictionary inside the archive gives each field's type, format, blank convention, source, and the noise mechanisms that apply to it. The deposit also carries a manifest of MD5 and SHA-256 digests (@tbl-release gives the MD5) and the configuration file that names every seed and design target, and the pipeline that built them will be archived under its own DOI<!-- OUTLINE run-list item 10: code DOI -->. A second build from the same configuration and the same source population reproduced all three files byte for byte.

## Population characteristics {#sec-population}

```{python}
#| label: population-descriptives
comp = pd.read_csv("results/registry_age_sex.csv")
fold = {"Multiracial or Other": "Other", "AIAN": "Other", "NHOPI": "Other", "Unknown": "Other"}
comp["race"] = comp["race_ethnicity"].map(lambda r: fold.get(r, r if r in ("White", "Latino", "Black", "Asian") else "Other"))

def share(file, mask):
    g = comp[comp["file"] == file]
    return g[mask(g)]["count"].sum() / g["count"].sum()

def race_shares(file):
    g = comp[comp["file"] == file].groupby("race")["count"].sum()
    return (g / g.sum()).reindex(["White", "Latino", "Black", "Asian", "Other"]).fillna(0)

female_reg, female_500k = pct(share("registry.csv", lambda g: g.sex == "Female"), 0), pct(share("finder_500k.csv", lambda g: g.sex == "Female"), 0)
over65_reg, over65_500k = pct(share("registry.csv", lambda g: g.age_start >= 65), 0), pct(share("finder_500k.csv", lambda g: g.age_start >= 65), 0)
under40_reg, under40_500k = pct(share("registry.csv", lambda g: g.age_start < 40), 0), pct(share("finder_500k.csv", lambda g: g.age_start < 40), 0)
race_reg = {k: pct(v, 0) for k, v in race_shares("registry.csv").items()}
race_500k = {k: pct(v, 0) for k, v in race_shares("finder_500k.csv").items()}

# the two finder files, compared on every share quoted in this section
_shares = lambda f: pd.concat([race_shares(f), pd.Series({"female": share(f, lambda g: g.sex == "Female"),
                                                          "over65": share(f, lambda g: g.age_start >= 65),
                                                          "under40": share(f, lambda g: g.age_start < 40)})])
finder_files_max_diff_pp = f"{100 * (_shares('finder_500k.csv') - _shares('finder_100k.csv')).abs().max():.1f}"

_n_pairs = len(pd.read_csv("results/example_pair.csv")["pair"].unique())
```

The simulated registry precisely matches the age and sex distribution of the cases reported to FCDS between 1995 and 2023. The agreement is within `{python} age_sex_max_dev` percentage points in each of the `{python} n_strata` age and sex strata. `{python} over65_reg` of registry records are people aged 65 or older at diagnosis and `{python} under40_reg` are under 40; `{python} female_reg` are female. The finder files have the age structure of the simulated population's Florida residents in 2040 instead: `{python} over65_500k` of the larger file are 65 or older, `{python} under40_500k` are under 40, and `{python} female_500k` are female.

By race and ethnicity, people in the registry are `{python} race_reg["White"]` White, `{python} race_reg["Latino"]` Latino, `{python} race_reg["Black"]` Black, `{python} race_reg["Asian"]` Asian and `{python} race_reg["Other"]` other or multiracial (American Indian and Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander, multiracial, and unknown), compared with `{python} race_500k["White"]`, `{python} race_500k["Latino"]`, `{python} race_500k["Black"]`, `{python} race_500k["Asian"]` and `{python} race_500k["Other"]` in the larger finder file. The two finder files differ from each other by at most `{python} finder_files_max_diff_pp` percentage points on every share reported in this section.

## Error structure {#sec-errors}

```{python}
#| label: error-structure
blank_by_file = json.load(open("results/pair_agreement.json"))["blank_share_by_file"]
pa100 = json.load(open("results/pair_agreement.json"))["finder_100k.csv"]["fields"]
FIELD_LABELS = [("first_name", "First name"), ("middle_initial", "Middle initial"), ("last_name", "Last name"),
                ("date_of_birth", "Date of birth"), ("sex", "Sex"), ("race_ethnicity", "Race/ethnicity"),
                ("street_number", "Street number"), ("street_name", "Street name"), ("unit_number", "Unit number"),
                ("city", "City"), ("state", "State"), ("zipcode", "ZIP code"), ("ssn", "SSN")]
ADDRESS = {"street_number", "street_name", "unit_number", "city", "state", "zipcode"}
def set_rate(file_kind, field):
    if field == "ssn":
        return no[file_kind]["ssn_missing"]
    if field in ADDRESS:
        return no[file_kind]["address_missing"]
    return 0.01  # pseudopeople's default leave_blank probability for every other field
def blank_cell(fname, kind, field):
    return f"{pct(blank_by_file[fname][field], 1)} ({pct(set_rate(kind, field), 0)})"
errors_100k_max_diff_pp = f"{100 * max(abs(pa[f][k] - pa100[f][k]) for f in pa for k in ('agree_when_both_present', 'blank_on_either_side')):.1f}"
unit_blank_reg = pct(blank_by_file["registry.csv"]["unit_number"], 0)
```

@tbl-errors gives the error structure field by field: the share of values that are blank in the registry and in the larger finder file, against the blanking rate set for each, and, among the `{python} overlap_500k_pairs` true matches, the share of pairs whose two records agree exactly when both have a value and the share with a blank on either side. Agreeing exactly means the two values are the same string, character for character. The error structure of the smaller finder file matches that of the larger on every figure in the table to within `{python} errors_100k_max_diff_pp` percentage points.

SSNs are blank in `{python} finder_ssn_missing` of finder records, the rate specified in our design, and in `{python} registry_ssn_missing` of registry records against a specified `{python} cfg_registry_ssn_missing`. The blanks beyond the amount desired in the registry were inherited from the pseudopeople source population, where SSN missingness varies with age and exceeds the target in the age groups that more frequently develop cancer. Blank SSNs also vary by race/ethnicity, and in the larger finder file `{python} ssn_blank_500k["Asian"]` of Asian and `{python} ssn_blank_500k["Latino"]` of Latino people's records have SSN missing, while `{python} ssn_blank_500k["White"]` of White people's are missing. In the registry the SSN missingness rates for Asian, Latino, and White people are `{python} ssn_blank_reg["Asian"]`, `{python} ssn_blank_reg["Latino"]` and `{python} ssn_blank_reg["White"]`. Of the SSNs present in the larger finder file, `{python} err_ssn_transposed` (`{python} err_ssn_transposed_share`) carry two adjacent digits swapped, and where a true match has an SSN on both sides the two agree in `{python} agree_ssn_500k` of pairs.

Names and dates of birth disagree more often than SSNs do. Among true matches with both values present, first names agree in `{python} agree_first_name_500k` of pairs, last names in `{python} agree_last_name_500k` and dates of birth in `{python} agree_dob_500k`, and each of these fields is blank on one side in about `{python} blank_first_name_500k` of pairs. Taken together, `{python} name_dob_all_agree_500k` of true matches agree exactly on first name, last name, and date of birth, and `{python} ssn_usable_500k` have an SSN on both sides that agrees. Street names agree in `{python} agree_street_name_500k` of pairs with both present and are blank on one side in `{python} blank_street_name_500k`; taking the six address fields together, the two records carry the same address in `{python} agree_address_500k` of the pairs in which no field is blank on one side only; the unit number is blank for `{python} unit_blank_reg` of registry records, because most addresses have none, and street numbers are blank above their set rates because some source addresses carry none.

Dates of birth are blank in `{python} dob_blank_reg` of registry records and `{python} dob_unparseable_reg` of those present do not parse as a calendar date (such as a month above twelve); `{python} doe_names_reg` registry records carry a Doe-pattern name (John or Jane Doe); no SSN in any file is a single repeated digit; and `{python} ssn_not_issuable_500k` SSNs in the larger finder file, and `{python} ssn_not_issuable_reg_word` in the registry, fall in ranges the Social Security Administration does not issue.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-errors
#| tbl-cap: "Error structure by field. Blank shares in the registry and the 500,000-record finder file, with the blanking rate set for each field in parentheses (FCDS's specification for SSN and address fields, pseudopeople's default elsewhere); and, among the 100,000 true matches, the share of pairs whose two records agree exactly when both have a value and the share with a blank on either side. Street and unit numbers include the blanks present in the source addresses, so they sit above their set rates."
#| output: asis
header = ["Field", "Blank, registry (set)", "Blank, finder file (set)", "True matches: agree when both present", "True matches: blank on either side"]
print("| " + " | ".join(header) + " |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|")
for f, label in FIELD_LABELS:
    print("| " + " | ".join([label, blank_cell("registry.csv", "registry", f), blank_cell("finder_500k.csv", "finder", f),
                             pct(pa[f]["agree_when_both_present"], 1), pct(pa[f]["blank_on_either_side"], 1)]) + " |")
```

## Linkage difficulty {#sec-difficulty}

```{python}
#| label: difficulty-values
u = fx["uniqueness"]
uniq_name_dob, uniq_lastname_dob, uniq_zip_dob_sex = pct(u["unique_name_dob"]), pct(u["unique_lastname_dob"]), pct(u["unique_zip_dob_sex"])
shared_fullname = pct(u["share_sharing_full_name"], 0)
unique_fullname = pct(1 - u["share_sharing_full_name"], 0)  # the complement: a full name no one else in the file shares
bl = fx["blocking"]["finder_500k.csv"]
n_pairs_naive = f"{bl['naive_pairs'] / 1e12:.1f} trillion"
pairs_block_dob = f"{bl['block_dob']['candidate_pairs'] / 1e6:.0f} million"
completeness_block_dob = pct(bl["block_dob"]["pairs_completeness"])
# the block keeps exactly the true matches whose dates of birth are present and agree on both sides (Table 2)
_dob_agree_both = pa["date_of_birth"]["agree_when_both_present"] * (1 - pa["date_of_birth"]["blank_on_either_side"])
assert abs(_dob_agree_both - bl["block_dob"]["pairs_completeness"]) < 0.005, "blocking completeness and Table 2 disagree"
pairs_block_ln_yob = f"{bl['block_lastname_initial_yob']['candidate_pairs'] / 1e9:.2f} billion"
completeness_block_ln_yob = pct(bl["block_lastname_initial_yob"]["pairs_completeness"])
r500_ssn_only_recall = rule("ssn_only", "recall")
r500_current_either_recall = rule("fcds_current_either", "recall")
strat = json.load(open("results/linkage_baseline_stratified.json"))["finder_files"]["finder_500k.csv"]["rules"]
def missed(rule_name, group):
    return 1 - strat[rule_name][group]["recall"]
def fm(rule_name, group):
    return 1 - strat[rule_name][group]["precision"]
groups = ["White", "Latino", "Black", "Asian", "Other or unknown"]
nd_missed_min, nd_missed_max = pct(min(missed("name_dob", g) for g in groups)), pct(max(missed("name_dob", g) for g in groups))
nd_fm_max = pct(max(fm("name_dob", g) for g in groups), 2)
ssn_missed_white, ssn_missed_latino, ssn_missed_asian = (pct(missed("ssn_only", g), 0) for g in ("White", "Latino", "Asian"))
best_missed_white, best_missed_asian = pct(missed("name_dob_or_ssn", "White")), pct(missed("name_dob_or_ssn", "Asian"))
lb100 = lb["finder_files"]["finder_100k.csv"]
rules100 = {r["rule"]: r for r in lb100["rules"]}
ladder_100k_max_diff = f"{100 * max(abs(rules[k]['recall'] - rules100[k]['recall']) for k in rules):.1f}"
baseline_threads = lb["node"]["duckdb_threads"]
# the Discussion's one-sentence summary of the ladder: recall range over all rules, and the precision floor
# once last name + date of birth, too loose a key to use alone, is set aside
ladder_recall_min = pct(min(r["recall"] for r in rules.values()), 0)
ladder_recall_max = pct(max(r["recall"] for r in rules.values()), 0)
ladder_precision_floor = pct(min(r["precision"] for k, r in rules.items() if k != "lastname_dob"), 0)
n_rules = len(rules)
```

We began by measuring how often a combination of fields uniquely identifies a person in the registry population. Among the `{python} registry_simulants` people in the registry, `{python} uniq_name_dob` have a first name, last name, and date of birth that no one else in the file shares, `{python} uniq_lastname_dob` have a unique last name and date of birth, and `{python} uniq_zip_dob_sex` a unique ZIP code, date of birth, and sex, while `{python} unique_fullname` have a full name that no one else in the file shares.

@tbl-ladder scores exact-agreement rules on the larger finder file against the key. Agreement on first name, last name, and date of birth links `{python} pct(r500_name_dob_recall)` of true matches at a precision of `{python} pct(r500_name_dob_precision, 2)`, and the SSN alone links `{python} pct(r500_ssn_only_recall)` at `{python} pct(r500_ssn_only_precision, 2)`. The two field sets from the FCDS Procedure Guide requirements behave differently as exact rules: name, SSN, and sex makes no false matches and finds `{python} pct(r500_fcds_min_ssn_recall)` of true matches, while name with month and year of birth and sex returns `{python} r500_fcds_min_monthyear_fp` false matches (`{python} r500_fcds_min_monthyear_fp_share` of the pairs it proposes). The rule that matches if either of the sets are the same finds `{python} pct(r500_fcds_either_recall)` of the true matches. The two sets from the FCDS current Data Linkage Record Layout, which both require the full date of birth, find `{python} pct(r500_current_either_recall)` together with no false matches. Our best rule of (Name and date of birth) or SSN, reaches a recall of `{python} pct(r500_best_recall)` at a precision of `{python} pct(r500_best_precision, 2)`, while (last name and date of birth) falls to a precision of `{python} pct(r500_lastname_dob_precision)`.

The `{python} n_rules` rules run in `{python} baseline_seconds_500k` seconds on the 500,000-record file with `{python} baseline_threads` threads on an eight-core allocation. The 100,000-record file gives the same picture: every rule's recall is within `{python} ladder_100k_max_diff` percentage points of the larger file's.


```{python}
#| label: tbl-ladder
#| tbl-cap: "Exact-agreement rules on the 500,000-record finder file, scored against the identity key. Guide rows are exact agreement on the field sets the FCDS Procedure Guide requires a submission to carry [@fdoh_fcds_procedure_guide_2007], and layout rows on the two sets of FCDS's current Data Linkage Record Layout [@fcds_linkage_layout]; neither is the registry's own matching procedure. Missed-match is one minus recall and false-match one minus precision."
#| output: asis
SHORT = {  # every rule the baseline scores, each union after its parts
    "name_dob": "First name, last name, date of birth",
    "name_dob_sex": "First name, last name, date of birth, sex",
    "ssn_only": "SSN alone",
    "fcds_min_ssn": "Guide set: name, SSN, sex",
    "fcds_min_monthyear": "Guide set: name, month and year of birth, sex",
    "fcds_min_either": "Either Guide set",
    "fcds_current_dob_ssn": "Layout set: name, sex, date of birth, SSN",
    "fcds_current_dob_address": "Layout set: name, sex, date of birth, ZIP code, and street address",
    "fcds_current_either": "Either layout set",
    "name_dob_or_ssn": "Name and date of birth, or SSN",
    "lastname_dob": "Last name and date of birth",
}
assert set(SHORT) == set(rules), "Table 3 must show every rule the baseline scores"
print("| Rule | Predicted pairs | True | False | Recall | Missed-match | Precision | False-match |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for key, label in SHORT.items():
    r = rules[key]
    print(f"| {label} | {n(r['predicted_pairs'])} | {n(r['true_positives'])} | {n(r['false_positives'])} | {pct(r['recall'])} | {pct(1 - r['recall'])} | {pct(r['precision'], 2)} | {pct(1 - r['precision'], 2)} |")
```

@fig-stratified splits three rules by the race/ethnicity recorded on the finder record. For first name, last name, and date of birth the missed-match rate is alike across groups, from `{python} nd_missed_min` to `{python} nd_missed_max`, and the false-match rate stays below `{python} nd_fm_max` in every group. The SSN rule differs by group: it misses `{python} ssn_missed_asian` of true matches for Asian people and `{python} ssn_missed_latino` for Latino people against `{python} ssn_missed_white` for White people, and the difference carries into the best simple rule, which misses `{python} best_missed_asian` of Asian true matches against `{python} best_missed_white` of White ones.

```{python}
#| label: fig-stratified
#| fig-cap: "Missed-match and false-match rates of three exact-agreement rules on the 500,000-record finder file, by the race/ethnicity recorded on the finder record, with the number of true matches in each group."
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.09, 3.1), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.3, 1]})
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.27, right=0.99, top=0.97, bottom=0.27, wspace=0.08)
handles = F.stratified_baseline(ax1, ax2)
fig.legend(handles=handles, loc="lower center", ncol=3, frameon=False, fontsize=7, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0))
```

Without blocking the two files present `{python} n_pairs_naive` record pairs. Blocking on the full date of birth leaves `{python} pairs_block_dob` candidate pairs and keeps `{python} completeness_block_dob` of true matches, the pairs whose dates of birth are present and agree on both sides (@tbl-errors); blocking on the first letter of the last name with the year of birth leaves `{python} pairs_block_ln_yob` and keeps `{python} completeness_block_ln_yob`.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

The files have three properties that no other open linkage test set we know of combines. They are the size of a large state registry and match the age and sex pattern of the Florida registry's cases. Every record carries an answer key, so linkage accuracy can be measured directly rather than estimated. And they are a direct download, which removes the barrier that has kept linkage test data out of reach: a container cannot file an access request, a classroom cannot wait for one, and a fixed, checksummed artifact makes this paper's own results reproducible in a way that a re-request cannot.

Deterministic linkage of these files with natural rules reaches recalls from `{python} ladder_recall_min` to `{python} ladder_recall_max` at precisions above `{python} ladder_precision_floor`, except for last name with date of birth alone, which is too loose a key to use by itself (@tbl-ladder). This is a baseline for more sophisticated probabilistic methods: the headroom above the best exact rule is what such a method has to show, and the blocking counts in @sec-difficulty are what its user needs to plan the compute. Exact name and date of birth links a smaller share of true matches here than rules of that kind achieve on real registry files [@li2006deterministic], because both sides carry noise, so the files are not easy by that standard, and where they are easier than life the reason is structural rather than a matter of rates.

There are at least four limitations in the simulated data. First, the simulation of a person's life between records is simplistic: a true match is one census record noised twice, so it has no address change, no aging, and no surname change between its two records, and address agreement among true matches is higher than any real registry sees. Whether this makes matching too easy is a fair question, and we do not yet know by how much; the address-change variant described below is the way to find out. Second, the noise is simplistic: it is independent across fields and files, and the mechanisms are limited to those described in @sec-noise, so the SSN carries no wrong digits and no relative's number. Third, diagnosis dates heap on three calendar years, which leaves age at diagnosis right but gives an unrealistic pattern of registry volume by year. Fourth, each file has one row per person, so within-file duplicate detection, the task on which registries are certified [@naaccr2026certification], is not easily tested with this resource. Each of these was a choice we made for simplicity, and each has a remedy among the extensions below.

The differences between race and ethnicity groups in @sec-difficulty are inherited from the source population, not injected by us. The noise is applied without regard to race or ethnicity, so the SSN rule misses more Asian and Latino true matches because fewer Asian and Latino people hold a Social Security number in the simulation; that is realistic in direction, but its size is the simulation's and not Florida's. Other features of the source population pull the other way: first names are not conditioned on race or ethnicity, names are drawn independently of one another, the rare-name tail is thinner than in life, and missingness within a field is largely at random where a real registry's is differential [@haddock2024simulated]. The warning that follows is the one this resource most needs to carry. A feature of the real problem that is absent here can change which tool ranks first, so a comparison on these files is necessary evidence about production performance but not sufficient, and a method that wins here should still be validated in situ [@alexandersson2024comparing].

This simulated data is designed for a specific entity resolution task and lacks the detail needed for adjacent tasks. There are no tumor variables and no vital status, and cancer is a bolt-on that changes neither mobility nor mortality in the simulation. There are no telephone numbers or email addresses, which real workflows increasingly use. The addresses are not real places and should not be geocoded. The names, addresses, and households are those of the United States around 2020, so a conclusion about a name comparator reached here does not carry to Brazil, to Australia, or to a registry in a non-Latin script.

Files like these have been used once already, when we supplied predecessors for the second author's feasibility study and package comparison at FCDS [@alexandersson2023splinkfcds; @alexandersson2024comparing], and rerunning that comparison on this public corpus, to see whether the ranking agrees with the registry's internal results, is the external-validity test still owed. We expect the files to serve a registry analyst comparing linkage solutions and a developer benchmarking a method without first obtaining confidential data, and a fixed corpus of this size also makes regression testing in continuous integration possible and gives research on differential linkage error a shared test bed.

Because the extract keeps every census year, several extensions are small changes to the draw. An address-change version would take an overlap member's registry record from an earlier census than the finder file, so that a known share of true matches moves house between their two records; a yearly observer would spread the diagnosis dates; the richer SSN errors the second author originally asked for, wrong digits and a relative's number, are a few lines of post-processing; and probabilistic baselines and a Parquet release beside the CSV are planned.

Nothing in these files is confidential, even though it may appear otherwise. The simulation was initialized from public-use microdata that already carries the Census Bureau's disclosure protections, and no confidential data set was fitted, so there is no confidential record to leak. There is still a risk of coincidental resemblance, however, and with millions of simulated Floridians some combinations of name, date of birth, and city will match real people by chance [@suchow2023coincidental]. The files also include syntactically valid Social Security numbers beside names, dates, and addresses, which makes them usable as seed material for synthetic identities and means that simulated records could contaminate a real registry system if someone loaded them carelessly. Our guardrails are the ordinary ones, prominent labeling as simulated, a versioned deposit with a withdrawal path, and a stated route for objections (@sec-access), and we should be plain that if someone objects to a simulated likeness of their name we have less recourse than a controller of real data would. One note on position: the first author is an author of the simulator whose release practices this section assesses, and the paper exists because of a recommendation the second author wrote; the conflict-of-interest statement carries the rest.

# Data Access {#sec-access}

The files are deposited on Zenodo under a DOI<!-- OUTLINE run-list item 10: dataset DOI to mint; reviewer URL for submission --> as the zip archive described in @sec-structure, three CSV files and the data dictionary, together with the manifest of MD5 and SHA-256 digests and the configuration file that names every seed and target. The pipeline that built them is archived under its own DOI and linked from the deposit<!-- code DOI and repository URL -->. Access is a direct download under a permissive license<!-- OUTLINE decision #9: CC0 or CC-BY -->, with no application, approval, registration, or data-use agreement, and the published digests let a user confirm that the files in hand are the files this profile describes. The files are UTF-8 CSV with a header row, blanks as empty fields, dates as `MM/DD/YYYY`, and SSNs as `ddd-dd-dddd`; a field is quoted only when it contains a comma, which is rare enough that some CSV readers need the quote character named explicitly. This profile describes version `{python} dataset_version`. Later versions will be deposited under new DOIs with earlier ones left in place, and the repository's policies govern withdrawal [@zenodo_policies]. The released files need no permission to use; rebuilding them, or building a different cut, requires the pseudopeople simulated population, which is available through its own request process [@keyes2026governance].

The two authors are the custodians of the resource, and the corresponding author is the contact for questions, corrections, objections, and proposals for extensions, which we welcome. We ask three courtesies of users: the data are simulated and must not be treated as describing real people; the addresses are not real places and should not be geocoded; and the SSNs, though well formed, were never issued to anyone and must not be loaded into any system that holds real records.

# Conclusions {#sec-conclusions}

We have built and released a set of simulated data files for testing record linkage in the size and shape of the challenge the Florida cancer registry faces: a direct download with a DOI, no application or approval, a published ground-truth key, and deterministic baselines to compare against. We hope the files will be used to benchmark and tune linkage software, to study differential linkage error, and to teach, with the caveat that a method which wins here should still be validated on real data before it goes into production. The transaction the files imitate, a government-held population-scale file, a researcher's cohort, a minimum set of identifiers, and no shareable ground truth, recurs in vital statistics, in cohort follow-up for drug epidemiology, and beyond health in social work and economics, and wherever it recurs the same kind of resource could be built. Let us know what you find!
